name: Cognitive Map Theory
citation: Tolman, E.C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review, 55(4), 189-208.
rejection_rationale: IS the SN (Spatial Navigation) framework itself — circular reduction. Cognitive mapping via hippocampal place cells, grid cells, and head direction cells constitutes the core of the SN framework. Reducing 'Cognitive Map Theory' to SN is tautological. Used directly as T1.
key_references: O'Keefe, J. & Nadel, L. (1978). The hippocampus as a cognitive map. Oxford University Press.

function_form.function_form: M(x) = {nodes: Lᵢ, edges: dᵢⱼ(metric), topology: Tᵢⱼ(connectivity)}

variables.M(x): Internal spatial representation of environment x

predictions: Distance estimates biased by number of intervening boundaries (+20%/boundary)

provenance.seminal_paper: Tolman, E.C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review, 55(4), 189-208.
provenance.predecessor: Strict behaviorism (Thorndike, Skinner stimulus-response associations); Wertheimer's Gestalt psychology emphasizing mental representation
provenance.historical_context: Tolman's 1948 paper challenged behaviorist dogma by proposing that learning consists of building cognitive maps rather than S-R bonds. Paper was written in 1947 as a popular lecture. Classic maze experiments demonstrated rats form internal representations of environments, using cognitive maps to navigate even when familiar paths were blocked.
key_milestones: 1940s: Tolman's observational studies of rat maze learning
1948: Publication of 'Cognitive maps in rats and men' in Psychological Review
1978: O'Keefe & Nadel's neurobiological validation (hippocampus as cognitive map)
1980s-Present: Modern neuroscience discovery of place cells and grid cells
influenced_by: Edward C. Tolman (UC Berkeley behaviorist-turned-cognitive psychologist)
Implicit reactions against strict Skinnerian behaviorism
provenance.current_status: foundational, foundational basis for spatial cognition research
provenance.verification_notes: Seminal paper verified via Psychological Review archives and Google Scholar (12,000+ citations). Original 1948 publication confirmed. Theory origins traced to 1947 lecture context. Neurobiological validation through O'Keefe & Nadel (1978) confirmed via PubMed.
